title: Predicates, Variables and Quantifiers
quickIdea: A predicate is a property or relation with a fixed number of slots; a quantifier binds a variable over a domain. Together they turn the open statement P(x) into a sentence that has a truth value.
remember: A predicate such as P(x) or R(x, y) is a statement about objects; its arity is the number of arguments it takes.
The domain (universe of discourse) is the non-empty set the variables range over. Unless a question says otherwise, all variables in one formula share the same domain.
Universal quantifier: for all x, P(x) is true when P holds for every element of the domain. Existential: there exists x with P(x) is true when it holds for at least one element.
An atomic formula is a predicate applied to terms. A well-formed formula is built from atomic formulas with not, and, or, implies, if-and-only-if and quantifiers.
A variable is bound inside the scope of its quantifier and free outside it. A sentence (closed formula) has no free variables, so it alone is true or false.
In propositional logic a variable ranges over {true, false}. In first-order logic it ranges over a domain of objects, and the predicate decides which objects satisfy it.

example.prompt: Domain: all students. S(x): x is a student. P(x): x passed. Is S(x) implies P(x) a sentence?
example.work: x occurs free, so the expression has no truth value until x is given a value or bound by a quantifier.
example.answer: No. Binding it gives a sentence: for all x (S(x) implies P(x)).

gateAngle: Every first-order question starts here: decide what the domain is, what each predicate means and which variables are bound. GATE 2020 Q.39, for instance, is decided by the scope of x inside each option.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: How many free variables does the formula (for all x R(x, y)) and Q(z) have?
variations.why: x is bound by the universal quantifier; y and z are not bound by any quantifier in the formula.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: With domain the integers, is the sentence 'for all x (x + 1 > x)' true, and does its truth depend on the domain?
variations.answer: True over the integers; and yes, the domain matters.
variations.why: Over the integers x + 1 > x always holds. The same formula read over a finite set with a greatest element would fail there, which is why the domain is part of the meaning.

trap.what: Treating a predicate as if it were a proposition with a truth value.
trap.why: P(x) has a truth value only once x is fixed or bound; P alone is a property, not a claim.
trap.counterexample: Domain {1, 2}, P(x): x is even. P(1) is false and P(2) is true, so 'P(x)' on its own is neither.

check.question: How many free variables are there in (for all x R(x, y))?
check.explanation: x is bound by the universal quantifier; y appears outside any quantifier that mentions it, so it stays free.
